note_claims.claim: The patient presents with pain below the right kneecap for 2 days.
The onset of pain was gradual and without a specific injury.
The patient plays football (training three times a week plus matches) and attends school PE.
Pain occurs during and after sport and when kneeling on the knee.
The patient reports no night pain or rest pain.
The patient reports no swelling, locking, or giving way of the knee.
The patient reports no pain in the hip or thigh.
The patient reports no fever or weight loss.
The patient's older brother had Osgood-Schlatter disease at a similar age.
The patient has no previous joint problems.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
The patient has no asthma or peptic ulcer disease.
There is a tender bony prominence over the right tibial tuberosity.
There is no knee effusion.
The X-ray of the knee is normal.
The patient has a full range of knee movement and stable ligaments.
Both hips have a full, pain-free range of movement.
The patient has a normal gait.
The impression is Osgood-Schlatter disease of the right knee.
There are no red flags.
The plan is activity modification guided by pain.
The plan is to ice the knee for 15 minutes after sport.
The plan is to take paracetamol or ibuprofen 400 mg up to three times a day with food as needed for pain.
The plan is to refer the patient to physiotherapy for stretching exercises for the quadriceps and hamstring muscles.
The plan is to review the patient if symptoms have not settled in 6 to 8 weeks.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports knee pain just below the kneecap.
The pain is in the right knee.
The pain has been present for about two months.
The pain started after football.
Patient trains three times a week and has a match on Saturdays.
Relative mentions school PE.
Pain occurs during and after football, and when kneeling on the knee.
Patient reports no night pain.
Pain is only felt after sport, not when resting.
Patient reports no swelling, locking, or giving way.
Limping only occurs after a match.
Relative states the patient's brother had a similar condition (Osgood-something) at age fourteen.
Relative confirms no previous joint problems.
Patient reports no regular medications or drug allergies.
Patient reports no asthma or stomach problems.
Clinician finds a tender bony lump just below the kneecap, identified as the tibial tuberosity.
Clinician examines the knee, noting no fluid, full range of movement, and stable ligaments.
Clinician examines both hips and finds full, pain-free range of movement.
Clinician diagnoses the condition as Osgood-Schlatter disease, explaining it is an irritation where the tendon from the kneecap attaches to the shin bone.
Clinician advises cutting down on football activity for a few weeks and letting pain guide activity levels.
Clinician recommends icing the knee for 15 minutes after sport and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen 400 mg up to three times a day with food for pain.
Clinician refers the patient to physiotherapy for stretching exercises for the thigh muscles.
Clinician sets a follow-up plan: return sooner if pain wakes the patient at night, the knee swells up, the patient gets a fever, starts limping all the time, or gets pain in the hip.
